decisions.q: What may the router use to judge how well each candidate model would answer a given request?
decisions.chosen: only signals a deployed router could observe at request time
decisions.rationale: Determined by the shipped baseline, not a free choice: evaluator/generic_policy.py:60 scores with a precomputed prediction head keyed by req.features['prompt_id'] (evaluator/benchmark/artifacts/generic_predictions.json), never req.quality. Reading the ground-truth req.quality dict the harness grades with would make the specialist an unreachable oracle and beat the baseline on information, not policy: a reward hack. Router code may read req.features and req.slo only.

decisions.q: How freely may the router serve a different model from the one the request named, given that the request permits it?
decisions.chosen: serve whichever model in the permitted set looks best on quality against price for this request
decisions.rationale: SETTLED BY THE MEASURED TRACE, not a default. All 6,504 train+val rows carry downgrade_ok:true and one identical equiv_class of all 12 models, so the permitted set is the whole fleet on every request. On the measured score/cost matrices the requested model is dominated for tenant A: qwen3-235b-a22b-2507 scores 0.5350 vs gpt-5's 0.5113 on val (0.5254 vs 0.4950 on train) at $0.002418 vs $0.025722 per request, a static utility of 0.5277 vs 0.4342. Fleet cost spread is 15.3-20.8x on A traffic and 112.7-123.4x on B traffic, so with the objective's -3.0*cost weight substitution is the widest single lever. cards/workload.json dimensions.quality_cost_landscape.

decisions.q: Among the providers that stock the chosen model, what decides which one gets the request?
decisions.chosen: remaining allowance and expected time-to-answer weighed together

decisions.q: When no provider can serve a request right now, does the router wait for capacity or refuse the request?
decisions.chosen: wait for capacity, with an explicit point at which the router gives up

decisions.q: How long may a request that cannot be served yet keep waiting before the router stops waiting on it?
decisions.chosen: until its own deadline runs out, and no longer
decisions.rationale: SETTLED BY THE MEASURED TRACE. A single fixed patience is provably wrong for one of the two tenants: A's whole budget is 2,500 ms from arrival while B's median queue slack is 532 s and its p90 is 391 s, and B's waves need 109-190 s of whole-fleet drain time that only deadline-length patience makes room for. Both tenants carry a deadline on every row (measured: 100% coverage, no row without an slo field), so tying patience to the request's own deadline is always defined. cards/workload.json dimensions.deadline_feasibility_headroom.

decisions.q: How should the router stay inside a provider's published request and token allowance?
decisions.chosen: subtract the request's own expected consumption from the published remaining allowance before dispatching
decisions.rationale: SETTLED BY THE MEASURED TRACE. Learning from a rejection is unaffordable for tenant A: a 429 costs a fixed 2,000 ms of a 2,500 ms budget, after which only prime can still land and only for prompts under 6,000 tokens, so 6.28% of A val rows (61/972, every tau2 row) can never recover from one throttle. The rejections are real, not hypothetical: A's val peak offers 181 requests per 60 s against prime's rpm 132 (137%) and courier's 150 (121%), and the env card records 19.4% of tenant-A requests taking at least one prime 429 under the reference router. Token allowances never bind (worst measured 60 s demand is 45% of the tightest tpm), so the subtraction that matters is against rpm and concurrency. cards/workload.json dimensions.fleet_headroom_at_peak.

decisions.q: After an attempt is rejected, should the next attempt go to a different provider or wait and try the same one again?
decisions.chosen: try a different provider first, waiting only when no alternative has room

decisions.q: Once a provider is known to be unavailable, when may the router send it real traffic again?
decisions.chosen: not before the announced end of its unavailability
decisions.rationale: SETTLED BY THE MEASURED TRACE. Outage exposure is not a corner case in this workload: measured against the val schedule, 41.3% of tenant B's val arrivals (286/693, an entire wave: 348.0-437.7 s inside the 300-420 s window) and 15.2% of tenant A's (148/972) land inside an announced prime outage, against 20.0% and 10.8% on train. With retry_grace 8, a policy that re-probes with real traffic burns the loss allowance nine dispatches into a window that lasts 120-150 s. The fleet publishes outage_until, so nothing needs to be inferred. cards/workload.json dimensions.outage_exposure.

decisions.q: Should a provider that is not formally unavailable, but has just been refusing or failing requests, be avoided for a while?
decisions.chosen: yes: a provider that has just been refusing or failing is passed over for a bounded period

decisions.q: Does the time left before a request's deadline change what the router does with it?
decisions.chosen: the deadline changes both the choice of provider and model and how long the request is willing to wait
decisions.rationale: SETTLED BY THE MEASURED TRACE. The two tenants' deadlines are 2,500 ms TTFT (A, 100% of 3,871 rows) and 600,000 ms end-to-end (B, 100% of 2,633 rows), a factor of 240, and the feasible action sets differ in kind, not degree: after one 429 A has 500 ms left, so only prime (ttft_base 400 ms) can still meet the SLO and only under 6,000 prompt tokens, while B's median request can queue 532 s and still finish. Measured: A first-try TTFT feasibility prime 98.05% / value 94.44% / courier 93.72% on val; B solo end-to-end feasibility 99.6-100% at every provider. cards/workload.json dimensions.deadline_feasibility_headroom.

decisions.q: What should the router do with a request that can no longer meet its deadline?
decisions.chosen: serve it anyway, as cheaply as the permitted set allows

decisions.q: May a tenant's router take capacity on the shared fleet that the other tenant would otherwise have used?
decisions.chosen: yes, up to whatever the provider's published limits allow
decisions.rationale: Default taken, and the harness makes it non-adversarial: evaluator/benchmark/replay_tenants.py replays ONE tenant trace at a time (trace_tenantA_val.jsonl / trace_tenantB_val.jsonl), so no specialist can observe or starve the other tenant inside a scored replay. Self-imposed headroom would only handicap; published provider limits remain the binding constraint.

decisions.q: Is what the router spends bounded by anything other than the traffic itself?
decisions.chosen: price is weighed against quality on every request, with no hard ceiling

decisions.q: Must two replays of the same trace produce the same decisions?
What bounds anything the router remembers between requests?
decisions.chosen: an explicit size or age limit on everything remembered

decisions.q: What must an operator be able to see after a request goes wrong?
decisions.chosen: which provider and model served it, how many attempts it took, and why each earlier attempt failed
